say.text: A 40-year-old with a 35% scald to the chest and both legs, seen 6 hours after the burn.
BP 85/50, pulse 130, urine 15 mL/h. Haematocrit has risen from 42 to 55. Temperature 37.2 °C. What type of shock is this?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what has left the circulation. Haematocrit rises when plasma leaves the vessels, and urine falls with it.
Not yet. Burns do get infected, but infection is a later threat, not the first cause of shock here.
Look at the haematocrit. Which way is it moving, and what does that say is leaving the blood?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-check the haematocrit: a rising value means plasma is leaving the vessels.

say.text: Septic shock is tempting because burns do get infected, and sepsis is a real killer after the first 48 to 72 hours.
But early burn shock is predominantly hypovolaemic: capillary leak moves plasma out, haematocrit rises and urine falls. Heart depression is an add-on.
Not yet. Burns do depress the heart a little, but a weak pump is a secondary factor early on.
Check the blood count and the urine. What do they say about the volume that is missing?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so start from the blood: a rising haematocrit points to plasma loss before pump failure.

say.text: Cardiogenic shock is tempting because the burn does depress myocardial function, and that part is real.
But the main problem is plasma loss: haematocrit rises and urine falls, so volume comes first. Burn shock is predominantly hypovolaemic.
Yes. A rising haematocrit and low urine output both mean plasma is leaving the circulation.
Burn shock is predominantly hypovolaemic, with some myocardial depression from mediators. The leak starts within minutes, peaks at 8 to 12 hours and runs on for up to 24 hours.
Still in the first 24 hours. The heart is a little depressed. What is the first-line treatment for this shock?

choices.label: Inotropes to support the failing heart
Titrated Ringer lactate, guided by urine output
Albumin infusion started at once, full dose
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the body is short of. The missing part is plasma volume, and it is the volume that goes back first.
Not quite. This is the pump-failure model: inotropes treat a weak heart, and the heart is not the main problem in burn shock.
What is missing from the circulation? Think about the haematocrit and the urine again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the cause first: burn shock is plasma loss, and heart depression is secondary.

say.text: Not quite. This is the albumin-first model. Albumin has a role in burn care, but not as the first fluid at the start.
Check the timing. What does classic practice give in the first hours, and when does colloid come in?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-check the timing: colloid waits for the capillary leak to settle.

say.text: Albumin is tempting because burns do lose protein, and albumin is a familiar fluid on the ward.
But the leak is the first problem, and classic Parkland gives crystalloid alone in the first 24 hours. Colloid comes later, about 8 to 24 hours, or when needs are very high.
Yes. Ringer lactate is the fluid of choice, and it is titrated to urine output rather than fixed.
Saline in large volumes causes hyperchloraemic acidosis, which is why Ringer lactate is preferred.
Classic Parkland, the first 24 hours. Which fluid is given?

choices.label: Ringer lactate, no colloid in the first day
Ringer lactate with albumin added from the start
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which formula this is. Then ask whether that formula puts colloid into its first day.
Not quite. This is the albumin-early model. Albumin is part of burn care, but classic Parkland does not give it on day one.
Read the choice again against the first 24 hours. What does the plan give, and what does it add?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-check the first 24 hours: classic Parkland is crystalloid alone, with colloid added later.

say.text: Yes. In classic Parkland the first 24 hours are crystalloid only. Colloid is considered once the leak settles, about 8 to 24 hours.
Which formula gives colloid as well as crystalloid in the first 24 hours?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about the formulae that have a colloid part. Then check whether classic Parkland is one of them.
Not quite. This is the mixing-up model: Parkland is easy to confuse with the colloid pair, because all the formulae share a 24-hour frame.
Read the choices again. Which formula has colloid in its first 24 hours, and which one does not?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pin the families: Evans and Brooke carry colloid, and classic Parkland does not.

say.text: Yes. Evans gives 1 mL colloid and 1 mL crystalloid per kg per % TBSA, plus dextrose in water.
Classic Parkland is the crystalloid-only formula, so the pair to remember is Evans and Brooke with colloid.
A forearm burn, mottled red and white. It hurts less than the skin around it, and it refills slowly when pressed.
What depth is it?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask two things: how much does it hurt, and does the skin blanch when pressed?
Not quite. This is the pain-equals-depth model. Less painful is not the same as painless.
Look at the sensation word in the stem again. Is the forearm insensate, or only less painful?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two: full thickness is painless, and this burn is only less painful.

say.text: Full thickness is tempting because a burn that has lost feeling sounds like the worst burn, and reduced pain seems to tell the same story.
Deep partial is less painful, mottled and slow to refill, and may need grafting. Full thickness is painless, dry, leathery and does not blanch.
Yes. Mottled, less painful and slow to refill fits deep partial thickness. Less pain is a clue to deep injury, not to full thickness.
Depth is read by pain, blanching and appearance together. Full thickness is dry, leathery and painless, and underestimating depth is the commonest error.
Simple erythema is not counted toward TBSA.
Which feature separates full thickness from deep partial thickness?

choices.label: Less painful than skin around it, slow refill
Slow healing over three weeks, with scarring
Painless, dry, leathery, and does not blanch
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start with sensation. Which description says the feeling is gone, and which only says the burn hurts less?
Not quite. This is the less-pain model again, now used to separate the two. Less painful is the deep partial clue, not the separator.
Ask whether sensation is gone, not whether it hurts less.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so sort the features: less painful points to deep partial, and painless points to full thickness.

say.text: Not quite. This is the healing-time model. Slow healing with scarring is a deep partial feature, so it does not separate the two.
On the day, judge sensation, blanching and dryness. Depth often only declares itself at 48 to 72 hours.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so use what you can see now, not how long the wound will take to heal.

say.text: Yes. Full thickness is painless, dry, leathery and does not blanch. Deep partial is less painful, with mottling and slow refill.
No hints now. A 50% scald to the trunk and forearm, 6 hours in. Haematocrit is rising, urine is 15 mL/h, and the forearm is mottled and less painful than the skin around it.
Which plan fits best?

choices.label: Septic shock, deep partial forearm, Ringer lactate titrated to urine
Hypovolaemic shock, deep partial forearm, Ringer lactate titrated to urine
Hypovolaemic shock, full thickness forearm, Ringer lactate titrated to urine
Hypovolaemic shock, deep partial forearm, Ringer lactate titrated, early albumin

say.text: Not quite. This is the septic-shock model. Infection is a later threat, and the rising haematocrit shows plasma loss first.
Which way is the haematocrit moving, and what does that say is leaving the circulation?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-check the shock type first, before the fluid.

say.text: Not quite. This is the pain-equals-depth model. The forearm is less painful, which points to deep partial, not full thickness.
Check the sensation in the stem again: is it painless, or only less painful?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate less pain from no pain before you choose.

say.text: Not quite. This is the early-albumin model. Albumin is part of burn care, but classic Parkland gives crystalloid alone in the first 24 hours.
Check the timing of colloid against the first day. Which hours does the plan cover?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recheck the first 24 hours: colloid waits for the leak to settle.

say.text: Yes. Hypovolaemic shock, a deep partial forearm, and Ringer lactate titrated to urine output: each part fits the picture.
The fluid is then steered hour by hour, not fixed by a formula.
